catalog_citation: Nzogi, Richard Kijjali. 2006. Lugwere Phonology Statement. Issue 1 (approved 15 June 2006). Entebbe: SIL Uganda / Lugwere Bible Translation and Literacy Association. 50 pp. (Glottolog hh:321009)
catalog_locator: Sec. 8 'Tone', p. 28 (opening paragraph, immediately after the 'Page 27 of 50' footer); Sec. 8.3 'Lugwere tone functional load', p. 35; cf. Sec. 6.1.2.2.1 item 5 'Penult contour tone protraction' + fn. 1, p. 13, and Sec. 8.2.3 note, p. 34
catalog_quote: Lugwere seems to have a register type of tone, and there are several pointers to the mora as the tone-bearing unit (TBU), including (i) existence of syllabic nasals in word-initial contexts which bear tone—just like all word-initial V-syllables, (ii) word-internal nasals on prenasalized segments compensatorily lengthening the vowels they follow (as is the case following palatalized and labialized segments), (iii) widespread litigious falling tone, both as a derived tone (in verbs and some adjectives) and as a melodic unit in single association (in nouns, adverbs, and some adjectives) both on phonemic short vowels (but conditioning phonetic length except word-final) and on monosyllabic bi-moraic vowel clusters (Heine & Nurse 2000, 60). Three distinct tones are apparent in Lugwere, out of which eight melodies: HL, LH, L, H, FH, FL, LF, and HF, are attested in the words and whose distribution in words upon the individual morae is highly word-specific. ... [8.3] First, assuming a one tone per syllable mora ordering, whether short, long, or clustered sequences whence the tone may be high, low, or falling, all Lugwere tones are contrastive. In other words, adjusting a single tone value on an individual syllable may change the meaning of the entire word, both in lexical items and grammatical categories.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Lugwere is described as a (register) tone language: H, L and a contrastive falling tone, mora = TBU, tone patterns lexically specified per word and used for lexical, grammatical (tense, polar questions) and discourse contrasts. The description contains no statement about word stress or a fixed prominence position; the only penult-related facts are phonetic vowel lengthening of a penultimate vowel under a falling (contour) tone and pre-NC lengthening. Kagaya (2005, 2006) independently analyses Gwere nouns with tone melodies (H, HL, L, LH, HLH) linked to a lexically specified 'accent syllable' (accent = tonal association site, syllable-based), likewise with no stress statement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tone: verbs form a single tone class (root melody LH in infinitives, H spreading rightward 'till the penultimate mora' in some inflected plural-subject forms, p.33); noun prefix tone polar to stem-initial tone (Kagaya); word-final H after L non-distinctive (Kagaya).
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms (infinitives with ku-, nouns with augment/class prefix) transcribed with tone throughout; Kagaya 2005 ch.3-4 also covers phrase-level tonal changes (final H > L on the word immediately before a verb). 'Penult contour tone protraction' (Nzogi p.13) applies word-internally except in diphthongs and not word-finally.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Lugwere/Gwere proper (gwer1238, ISO gwr), Pallisa/Budaka districts. Nzogi 2006 is a native-speaker SIL/LBTLA statement based on a 1000+ item wordlist; Kagaya's informant is from Lerya-Kakule, Budaka County. Not to be confused with Lulamogi or Lusoga (Hyman's tonal work), which are separate Glottolog languoids.

new_statements.quote: In Chapter 1, the author discusses the unit of accent place, i.e., whether an accent of a morpheme is placed on a syllable or a mora is discussed, and as a result, a syllable is adopted as the unit of accent place. [p.123] [...] five tone melodies (TM), i.e., H, HL, L, LH and HLH are proposed for noun stems (including infinitives) and H is assumed as for an initial vowel of a noun. [p.124] || アクセント (トーンメロディ中の指定された一つのトーンが連結する位置) は一見 TBU 単位に配列されているように見える [...] 従って, アクセント配列単位を TBU とするよりも音節とする方がより簡潔であり, 斉一なシステムを構成できる。 [p.127]
new_statements.translation: Japanese part: 'The accent (the position at which the one designated tone of the tone melody links) at first sight appears to be placed by TBU [tone-bearing unit] [...] Therefore, taking the syllable rather than the TBU as the unit of accent placement is simpler and yields a uniform system.'

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with Nzogi 2006 that Lugwere is a tone language with no stress statement; refines it by giving a tonal-accent (tone-melody + accent-syllable) analysis, five stem melodies, syllable as the accent-placement unit, and the non-distinctive final H. Nzogi's 'mora = TBU' and Kagaya's 'accent placement counts syllables' are compatible because Kagaya also counts TBUs by mora. Kagaya's 'accent' must not be read as stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Gwere is analysed as a tone language: noun stems carry one of five lexical tone melodies (H, HL, L, LH, HLH), the initial vowel is H, prefix tone is the polar opposite of the following stem's first tone, and each stem has a lexically specified 'accent syllable' where the first tone of its melody links (association conventions (10a-d), p.175). Kagaya's 'accent' is this tonal anchor, not stress: the paper never says anything about word stress in Gwere (the single occurrence of ストレス, p.136, is a general remark that Pulleyblank's peripheral-element idea 'originally came out of stress research and tone research'). Ch.1 argues that the accent-placement unit is the syllable, while the TBU is the mora (short vowel = 1 TBU, long vowel = 2 TBU). A final H after L(s) is non-distinctive ('modifying non-distinctive tone', 5.2, pp.165-166), a trait shared with Soga but absent in Ganda.
new_statements.exceptions: Swahili loanwords (all of the LHLH type, 5.3, p.166) are integrated with the accent syllable on the penult, mirroring Swahili penultimate lengthening; word-final H changes to L before a verb (rule 45) and before a numeral without initial vowel (rule 54).
new_statements.identity_note: Kagaya 2005 calls the language 'Gwere' (Guthrie E17, Nyoro-Ganda group) and its data come from two speakers born in Budaka County, Pallisa district (Lerya-Kakule and Manyoni villages), collected 2001-2003; the dictionary states the Bagwere live in Budaka, Kibuku and Pallisa districts. No dialect split is described in either work.

tone_statements.citation: Sæbø (Saeboe), Lilja Maria. 2025. The Lugwere verb system. DPhil thesis, University of Oxford (Balliol College; deposited in ORA 2026-07-03, record creator 'Saeboe, LM'). xxi + 566 pp. (587 PDF pages). doi:10.5287/ora-dqowggykj
tone_statements.quote: Lugwere is a tonal language, and it has both lexical and grammatical tone. The grammatical tone can be divided into two categories, which I term morphological and morphosyntactic tone. [...] Lexical tone is found on nouns, adverbs and adnominal elements, which have inherent, contrastive tonal melodies. Verb stems, on the other hand, have no inherent lexical tone. [3.2.1] A syllable can carry one of four surface tones: high, low, falling or, in rare cases, rising (Nzogi (2006) describes Lugwere as having only high, low and falling tones). [...] In verbs, it is clear that all the surface tones can be explained by two underlying tones; a low and a high.
tone_statements.locator: Ch. 3 'Phonology', sec. 3.2 'Suprasegmental phonology' (opening) and 3.2.1 'Surface and underlying tones', pp. 101-102; cf. 3.2.2 'The tone-bearing unit' pp. 103-105, 3.2.11 'Lexical tone' p. 113ff, 3.2.12 'Morphological tone' p. 123, 6.10.1 'A discussion of the analysis of tonal melodies' p. 319
tone_statements.n_tones: 2 underlying (H, L); 4 surface (H, L, falling, rare rising) + downstep

sources.note: Nothing: the words 'stress' and 'accent' (in the prosodic sense) do not occur anywhere in the 50 pages. Sec. 8 'Tone' (pp. 28-35) describes Lugwere as a register tone language with three tones (H, L, Falling), mora as TBU, eight melodies, tone fully contrastive lexically and grammatically (8.3, p.35). Only penult-related remark is phonetic: 'Penult contour tone protraction' = half-lengthening of a penultimate vowel bearing a falling tone (p.13, fn.1), and vowels lengthen before NC. No statement of word stress or fixed prominence.

sources.note: Image scan; scanned front matter ('Note of the Gwere Language', pp. iii-ix). Sec. 1: 'A vowel before a prenasalized consonant /NC/ tends to be long. Especially, it is definitely long when the vowel before a prenasalized consonant is placed on the penultimate syllable of a word.' Sec. 3 'Tone': nouns carry tone melodies H, HL, L (2005: also LH, HLH) whose first tone links to a lexically defined 'accent syllable'; final H after L is 'redundant'; prefix tone polar to stem TM. 'Accent' here is the tonal association site, not stress; no stress statement.

sources.note: Image scan (Japanese); scanned pp.123-127 and 170-176 plus English abstract. Ch.1 (p.127) defines アクセント as 'トーンメロディ中の指定された一つのトーンが連結する位置' (the position where the designated tone of the tone melody links) and argues the syllable, not the TBU/mora, is the unit for locating this accent (e.g. infinitives rise in pitch from the stem-second syllable regardless of syllable weight). Purely tonal analysis (5 tone melodies, tonal polarity of prefixes, non-distinctive final H); no mention of stress (ストレス/強勢 absent in scanned pages).

sources.note: First-hand analysis: Lugwere is a tonal language with lexical and grammatical (morphological + morphosyntactic) tone. Four surface tones on the syllable (H, L, falling, rare rising; revises Nzogi 2006's three), all reducible to two underlying tones H and L; downstep (sec. 3.2.5), floating tones, tone spreading, tonal polarity and assimilation. TBU discussion: mora behaves as TBU in nouns, syllable in verbs (contours only on 'defective' short verb forms).
